content: The University of Aberdeen School of Medicine is part of the College of Life Sciences and Medicine at the University of Aberdeen. The medical school has a long history, dating back to the founding of King’s College in 1495, making it the first English-speaking medical school in the world. Currently, the medical school is primarily located at the Foresterhill site in Aberdeen. However, undergraduate anatomy teaching also takes place at Marischal College. The main teaching hospitals include Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, Aberdeen Maternity Hospital, the Royal Aberdeen Children’s Hospital, Woodend Hospital, and the Royal Cornhill Hospital. Additional teaching is conducted in Inverness at Raigmore Hospital, in Elgin at Dr. Gray’s Hospital, and at other hospitals across the Highlands and Islands. The Dean of the School is Professor Michael Greaves, a Consultant Haematologist. The school has two active Regius Professorships: the Regius Chair of Medicine and the Regius Chair of Surgery. The Regius Chairs of Midwifery and Anatomy are currently inactive. The school offers three undergraduate degree programs: 1. Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MB ChB) 2. Bachelor of Science in Medical Science (BSc Hons) 3. Bachelor of Science in Health Science (BSc Hons) Postgraduate degrees are available as taught courses, typically leading to a Master of Science (MSc), or as research degrees at the master’s (MSc, MRes, ChM) or doctoral (PhD, MD) levels. The MB ChB program is a five-year course, similar to other Scottish medical schools. The curriculum is divided into four phases: Phase I: Fundamentals of Medical Sciences (Year 1) Students begin with a Basic Science in Medicine course, which includes lectures in physiology and biochemistry. This is followed by system-based lectures and anatomy sessions addressing normal physiological aspects, complemented by practical sessions. A Community Course occurs weekly, where students visit local general practices and interact with community health services, such as visiting families with newborns. Communication skills are developed through small group tutorials and role-playing in the Clinical Skills Centre. A four-week Student Selected Component (SSC) allows students to research healthcare topics in depth. This phase focuses on foundational medical sciences, self-directed learning, and professional communication. Phase II: Principles of Clinical Medicine (Year 2 and two-thirds of Year 3) This phase begins with a Principles of Disease course, followed by system-based lectures on abnormal physiology and diseases. The Community Course continues, now emphasizing disease, disability, and rehabilitation. Students participate in Medical Interviewing and Communications Courses, which include role-playing with simulated patients and video feedback. Clinical skills are practiced twice weekly in the Clinical Skills Centre and hospital wards. Two four-week SSCs allow students to explore topics such as the molecular basis of medicine and population-based diseases. This phase introduces students to disease processes, patient impact, and basic diagnostic and management principles. Phase III: Specialist Clinical Practice (Final third of Year 3 and Year 4) This phase begins with an SSC on ethical issues, followed by nine five-week clinical blocks organized by body systems (e.g., alimentary, urinary) and multi-disciplinary areas (e.g., Child Health, General Practice). Students observe the application of Phase II theory in clinical settings, interacting closely with patients and their families. This phase emphasizes diagnostic and management skills for patients of all ages with conditions affecting various body systems. Phase IV: Professional Practice (Year 5) This phase is an apprenticeship year, preparing students for professional practice as Foundation House Officers. Students complete four courses, focusing on clinical areas of personal interest while practicing core medical skills under supervision. A project-based elective, often conducted overseas, allows students to explore a medical topic in depth. Intercalated Degree At the end of Phase II, students may opt to undertake a one-year intercalated Honours Biomedical Science degree. This program includes both taught and research components, allowing students to study a specific area of biomedical or clinical science in depth. Each student completes an individual research project, gaining skills in research methodology and critical evaluation. The Aberdeen Medical Society (Medsoc) is the oldest student society at the University of Aberdeen, with over 600 members. It organizes annual social events such as Beerienteering, the Medsoc Ball, and a Fashion Show, with proceeds supporting local children’s charities. The society is managed by Phase III students, with Miss Kirsten Wade currently serving as president. The school comprises several departments, including Child Health, General Practice, Medical Microbiology, Mental Health, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Pathology, Public Health, Radiology, and Surgery. It also houses research units such as the Centre for Rural Health, the Dugald Baird Centre, and the Health Economics Research Unit. Notable alumni include Robert Brown (discoverer of Brownian motion), Sir Graeme Catto (former president of the General Medical Council), John James Richard Macleod (co-discoverer of insulin and Nobel Prize winner), Sir Patrick Manson (known as the Father of Tropical Medicine), and Sir Alexander Ogston (discoverer of Staphylococcus aureus).
